title: The Word made flesh (John 1:14)
hookLine: God became human, born and hungry and tired

lines: GOD KNOWS IT FROM THE INSIDE.
cards: Think about your body today. Maybe you woke up stiff. Maybe you were hungry by eleven.

Maybe your feet hurt, or your eyes are tired from a screen, or you just need a nap. Ordinary, slightly embarrassing, completely human. Now here's a thought that has startled people for two thousand years.
Christians say God knows exactly what that feels like. Not from a distance, like a doctor reading a chart. From the inside.

God was once a baby who needed feeding in the night, a boy who scraped his knees, a man who walked until his feet were sore and sat down by a well, worn out. Today's word names it, in one short line from John's Gospel.

teach.b: Incarnation comes from Latin: in, plus caro, carnis, flesh. Same root as carnival and chili con carne. In-flesh-ment.

John's Gospel begins with a poem about the Word, who was with God and was God, through whom everything was made. Then, in verse fourteen, the poem lands with a thud: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us."
Flesh. John could have said body, or human nature. He chose the plainest, earthiest word there is.
The Greek is sarx: meat, skin, the part of you that gets hungry and bleeds.

teach.h: HE PITCHED HIS TENT AMONG US.
teach.b: And dwelt, in Greek, is literally pitched his tent. God camped among us. The Gospels don't flinch.
Jesus is born and laid in a feeding trough.
After forty days in the desert, Matthew says simply, he was hungry. In John, "Jesus therefore, being wearied with his journey, sat thus on the well." He sleeps through a storm in a boat.
At his friend's grave, in the shortest verse in the King James Bible: "Jesus wept." Christians of every church see the incarnation as the center of the whole story, and Christmas is its feast.
It means God didn't fix the world from outside.

teach.h: AND THE WORD WAS MADE FLESH, AND DWELT AMONG US.
teach.b: God came in. And your body, with its hunger and its tiredness, isn't beneath God. It was worth becoming.
Early Christians put it this way: God took on everything human, so that everything human could be healed. Tomorrow, the other half: this tired man by the well was also, fully, God.

how: Christians celebrate the incarnation at Christmas, and in many churches people bow or kneel at the words "and was made man" in the Nicene Creed.

o: God appearing to people in a vision
God becoming a human being, flesh and all
a soul being reborn into a new body

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: the shortest verse in the KJV

s: the Gospels show Jesus as never hungry or tired
he's hungry in the desert, worn out at the well, asleep in a boat, weeping at a grave.
incarnation and carnival share a root
both come from the Latin for flesh.
John uses a polite, abstract word for Jesus's body
he uses sarx, the plainest, earthiest word: flesh.

games.q: you're writing the opening of a Gospel. you've said the Word was with God and was God. now: how do you say he became human?
o: the Word took on a human nature.
the Word appeared in the likeness of a man.
games.why: John chose the earthiest word there is: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us."

practice: Move your attention slowly up from your feet: legs, belly, hands, shoulders, face, and wherever there's tiredness or ache, don't fight it; just notice it, kindly.
This body gets hungry and tired, and it's also where your whole life happens. If you pray, thank God for coming close enough to share it; if you don't, thank your body for carrying you this far.

wordCard.voice: Incarnation. From the Latin for flesh. The Christian belief that God became human in Jesus: born, hungry, tired.

orig.note: Greek: flesh, the stuff of a body that gets hungry and bleeds. John 1:14's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the word became flesh. Three hundred days now, and i'm glad for every one.
